Q: Taking address of a temporary is allowed if the function's result is consumed A:

C++ 7.6.2.2 final working draft:

The operand of the unary & operator shall be an lvalue of some type T. The result is a prvalue.

In auto v = foo(&bar());, the operand to the unary & operator is not an lvalue and this is therefore invalid.

Q: Should a C++ logger write method be defined as const? A:

There is always some gray area. Your Logger class could have a private unique_ptr<LoggerState> member and the counter could be part of this LoggerState. Now the Logger could indirectly modify the counter without mutating its own data (and without the need for a mutable member). But users of the Logger class would not know. Using the const Write method would seem to modify the object. But actually another object is modified. So it depends on what you define what the state of your Logger is logically. Does the counter belong to this logical state of the Logger or not? That makes the Write method non-const or const.

Of course the Loggers Write method changes some state, maybe the state of the screen or log file, but not necessarily its own state. For example the LoggerState object and its counter may be shared by multiple Logger instances (e.g. via shared_ptr instead of unique_ptr). Then it's easier to decide, whether the counter belongs to the Logger or not, whether the Write method must be non-const or const. So that's the question: Does the Write method change the Logger itself or does it change something else?

Q: Install R with shared library in OSX - liblzma library missing A:

After brew install xz I still was getting the same error. Explicitely including the LD and CPP paths did the trick:

./configure CPPFLAGS="-I/opt/homebrew/include" LDFLAGS="-L/opt/homebrew/lib" --enable-memory-profiling --enable-R-shlib --with-x=no

Q: Using gpg in docker build step, is there an easier way or option to autokill the agent? A:

I have been struggling with importing GPG keys inside docker container too, although in a bit different context (building kernel inside archlinux container). The only solution I came up with after some unsuccessful googling is very similar to something you've already written:

FROM archlinux

...

ADD ./keys/pgp /home/arch/kbuild-keys
RUN gpg --import /home/arch/kbuild-keys/*.asc && gpgconf --kill all

A bit of explanation

According to https://man.archlinux.org/man/gpg.1.en#use the gpg command always uses agent and apparently there's no way to prevent it from at least trying to use it. There is the --no-autostart option though, which looks helpful, but isn't in our case:

ADD ./keys/pgp /home/arch/kbuild-keys
RUN gpg --import --no-autostart /home/arch/kbuild-keys/*.asc

Q: How To Sync Hugging face Repo in Git Without Error In Windows A:

The hf CLI login does not automatically configure Git credentials. You need to set up the credential helper"

git config --global credential.helper store

huggingface-cli login

Then update your remote URL to include your username.

git remote set-url origin https://YOUR_USERNAME@huggingface.co/axonura/axonura-X1
git push

When prompted for password, use your HF access token

Q: Login User not bound to the initially resolved user in CIBA A:

The CIBA spec allows room for the authenticating user to be different to the user represented by the login_hint. In some use cases, like a corporate team who can approve access to an AI agent, that might possibly make sense.

In the majority of use cases the user identifiers should be the same. For example, a call center application that uses CIBA needs to get tokens to act on behalf of the expected user. Many OPs are likely to enforce that behavior, or allow you to apply custom logic to validate conditions before issuing tokens.

The simplest UX pattern is for the OP to use login methods that do not require typing a username. For example, the OP can receive the hint, look up the user account and read the user's email or phone, then trigger email or SMS authentication.

To avoid incorrect approvals, present a clear OAuth consent screen to the user, which should display user and client details, along with token permissions (scopes and claims) being requested.

The binding_message parameter is also useful, to keep the user informed with a runtime message. For example, BankID is a free login service in Nordic countries where users typically login via a mobile app. Its CIBA flow allows the display of a binding message in the app during user authentication and consent.

Q: How can I detect whether a Linux process has been configured as a child subreaper? A:

I know it's an old question, but still.

I have actually wondered that myself and am glad that someone else had considered it somewhat useful. I searched the Linux source tree and it doesn't seem to be exposed through procfs or anywhere else, so I decided to tweak the kernel procfs code a bit to add this functionality as an exercise to start getting familiar with linux kernel code. You can take a look at the simple patch I've created: https://github.com/kevwargo/arch-kernel/blob/a23fe90e2f7d53cfe327cb2c04f755eed5b17e5a/kvz-kernel.patch. It creates a new readonly file entry in the /proc/<pid> dir which contains two binary values: is_subreaper and has_subreaper, where the latter, if non-zero, means that the process has an ancestor which is a child subreaper.

It was a cool bit of playing around with linux code, but I somehow doubt that it would be accepted to the mainline, because there doesn't seem to be a good use-case for that. Or maybe you have a legitimate use-case, then it's worth considering.
